title: The Registry Is Not Your Allowlist
excerpt: The 1 November 2026 catalog file lists 14,137 MCP servers. Six adult-content tools were in it because a registry import is not a review. Official means a name was registered.
coverImageAlt: A stack of official registry cards, one of them adult content, beside a short team allowlist that stops that card
newsletterSubject: The official MCP registry is not your allowlist.
newsletterIntro: A registry import will keep handing you servers you would never put in mcp.json. On the 1 November 2026 snapshot, six adult-content listings were in the file. The public directory hides them. That is a slug list, not a policy.
newsletterPullQuote: Official means a name was registered. It does not mean a human decided an agent should call the tool.
contentHtml:
The argument in MCP right now is not whether the protocol is real. It is whether a public registry is a store, a phone book, or a dump.

Teams keep treating “in the official registry” as “fine to connect.” It is not. A registry records that someone claimed a name. Your allowlist records that a person at your company decided an agent may call that tool. Those are different jobs, and the gap between them is where the ugly listings live.

What showed up when we actually read the catalog

The catalog file dated 1 November 2026 (14:39 Europe/Paris) contains 14,137 MCP servers. 383 of them store at least one tool. The rest are names, blurbs, and a Connect button.

Six of the 14,137 are adult sexual content. They arrived the way most of the long tail arrives: an import from the public registry, filed under ordinary categories such as Search & Web and Dev Tools. The set is a porn-video search, an adult short-video search, a companion chat that sends pictures and drives a connected toy, an adult image and video generator, an API onto creator platforms, and a directory of places to list NSFW apps.

They are hidden on the public directory. The raw snapshot still contains them until a full catalog refresh rewrites the file. Hiding them is a slug blocklist, six names long. A seventh server with a new slug walks straight past it.

The same week, someone submitted a remote server with no sign-in whose tools search an escort directory. It was not published. The submission described itself as Search & Web. The pitch was the part people are arguing about: Streamable HTTP, no account, every result linked back to the source site. Convenient. Also a tool an agent can call.

The controversial part

A lot of builders want the registry to stay neutral. Protocol people say a namespace should not have a morals board. If a directory starts refusing listings, someone will call it a censor, and they will not be entirely wrong about the power. The next refusal might be a security tool, a jailbreak research server, or a gambling-odds API that a trading desk actually wants.

The other side is simpler, and it is the one this directory is on. An MCP server is not a link. A search result sends a human to a page. A tool call is the agent doing the thing. Putting a porn search or an escort search in the same install path as Postgres means the next mcp.json can pick it up because a registry said the name was valid.

Neutrality is a reasonable rule for a namespace. It is a bad rule for an allowlist, and it is a bad default for a directory that already renders a Connect button.

We drew one line and left another one visible, on purpose. Sports-odds servers, lottery-number tools, and a tool that opens picks inside a US sportsbook are still in the catalog. The sponsored-placement terms ban gambling ads. The public directory does not, yet. If that sounds inconsistent, it is. The adult-content cut was the one we would not ship. The gambling cut is still a decision, not a law of the protocol.

“No sign-in” is the feature and the hole

Remote MCP is winning because chat clients cannot see your laptop. The listing that converts says Streamable HTTP and no API key. For a read-only public dataset, that can be honest. For anything that searches people, spends money, or writes, “no sign-in” means there is no user to revoke and no scope to shrink.

The escort submission led with that sentence. So do a lot of legitimate servers. The words do not tell you which one you are looking at. Read the tools. list_tables and search_listings are both “no sign-in” until you see what they return.

Auth is still the other fight, and it is not settled: pasted personal tokens, OAuth that asks for the whole account, and headers that quietly carry secrets. We have written that up in paste-a-key is dead and don’t put secrets in MCP headers. The new twist is that “no key” is now a marketing bullet, not only an omission.

Tool text is an instruction channel

The second argument, quieter and worse, is that tools/list is a prompt. Names and descriptions are what the model uses to decide what to call. A listing can look like a docs page and still carry “ignore previous instructions,” hidden Unicode, or a comment the human UI never shows. Our submission scan looks for those patterns. It does not understand “this tool searches escorts.” A clean scan and a prohibited product are different failures.

That is why there is still no SAFE badge. A handshake says the endpoint answered. It does not say the tool is fit to run. Not safe — just honest is the longer version. The methodology is the scoring, and it is not a safety score.

What a slug list will not do

After the six removals we kept the slugs in data/mcp-listing-blocklist.json. The directory hides them on read. The Top 100 build skips them. The next full import drops them before it writes the catalog file.

That list does not read a new submission. Approving a listing does not check it. The escort server was dismissed under its own slug, and that slug is not on the list, because it was never published. Resubmit it under another name and the blocklist shrugs.

A blocklist is how you stop a known bad name from crawling back in through the importer. It is not how you notice the next one. Someone still has to read the tools.

What to put on the allowlist anyway

  1. Start from the Top 100 or a capability search, not from “it is in the registry.”
  2. Require a real tool surface. On this snapshot, 383 listings have one. The other 13,754 are not an install plan.
  3. Match transport to the client. Remote chat cannot call localhost. Local stdio is not your company identity story. Stdio, HTTP, hosting, and secrets.
  4. Treat “no sign-in” as a fact to explain, not a badge.
  5. Put the survivor on a list a human owns. Policy before plugins. Discovery can shortlist. It should not be the allowlist. Connect it if you want search from inside the agent.

Payment does not cross that line either. A sponsored slot is a label above the list. Rank is not for sale.

Quick answers

Is the official registry unsafe?

It is unreviewed. Unsafe is a property of a tool in a context. “Official” only means the name was registered.

Will Influzer list every registry server?

The import is wide. The public directory is not a promise that we endorse the tool. Adult sexual-content servers we have identified are hidden. A new slug is not caught until someone notices it.

Why are betting tools still listed?

Because we have not applied the ad-policy gambling ban to organic listings. That is an open choice, not an oversight we are pretending is a principle.

Does a handshake mean the server is allowed?

No. live_ok means initialize and tools/list succeeded. Read the methodology before you treat a grade as permission.

Where should a team start?

A short allowlist. The directory for candidates. Seven questions before the config is shared.

Related

  • Most MCP servers are still demoware
  • Not safe — just honest
  • Policy before plugins
  • Your website is not an MCP server
  • Submit a server if the useful one is missing. A submission is a review queue, not an automatic install.

Final thought

The registry will keep growing, and it will keep accepting names a directory should not hand to an agent. That is what a neutral namespace does.

Official means the name exists. Allowed means you decided the tool may run.

Keep the allowlist short. Read the tools. Do not let a Connect button finish the argument.
